text: I was halfway through watering the tomatoes when Gerald leaned over the hedge holding a roll of orange survey tape. Gerald, who had spent fifteen years telling anyone at the block party that fences were the death of a real neighborhood. I let the hose drift until it was soaking my own shoes. "You want a what?" I said, and my voice came out a full octave higher than I meant it to. He nodded, perfectly calm, and explained he'd already called the contractor, already picked cedar, already marked the posts. I just stood there blinking, water pooling around my ankles, trying to fit this man in front of me with the one who had once lectured the HOA for forty minutes about open lawns. My mouth kept opening and closing like a goldfish. "Since when?" I finally managed. He shrugged and said his new grandson liked to wander. I laughed, a short bark of disbelief, and then had to turn off the hose because I'd completely forgotten it was running.

Amara had braced herself for an argument when the knock came. Mr. Delacroix next door had been grumbling about her chickens for months, and the clipboard in his hand looked like the opening move of a long war. Instead he turned the page toward her and tapped a sketch. The fence would sit two feet inside his own property line, he said, not hers, and he would pay every cent. Amara's eyebrows shot up so high her forehead ached. She read the drawing twice, then a third time, her finger tracing the dotted line as though it might move. "You're giving me two feet of your yard?" she asked, the words tumbling out in a rush. He rubbed the back of his neck and said the hens could use the room. Amara caught herself gripping the doorframe. She kept glancing from the sketch to his face and back again, searching for the catch, the hidden clause, the joke, and finding nothing but a tired old man who apparently liked her chickens after all.

The surveyor's van pulled up at eight, which I expected, because my neighbor Lorraine had told me she wanted the new fence done before her daughter's wedding. What I didn't expect was the young woman in the reflective vest walking straight past the old property stakes and planting a flag in the middle of my vegetable bed. I put down my coffee. Then I picked it back up, because my hands needed something to hold. "That can't be right," I said. She showed me the map on her tablet. The line ran right through my garden shed. My shed, the one my father built the summer I turned nine, sat almost entirely on Lorraine's side. I actually took a step backward, as if the ground under me had changed owners while I stood on it. Lorraine came out in her bathrobe and stared at the flag too, her mouth hanging open. For a long moment neither of us spoke. Then she let out a nervous giggle, and so did I.

Tomasz Wierzbicki had agreed to the fence mostly to keep the peace. When the crew from across the street began unloading lumber, he wandered out with his cane to supervise, expecting the usual pressure-treated pine. He stopped dead at the edge of the driveway. The boards were weathered gray, silvered with age, and on the end of one he could make out a faded painted letter, a red W. His breath caught. He shuffled closer and ran his thumb over the paint, then over another board, and another, turning them in the sun. These were planks from his father's barn, the one torn down on the old farm upstate thirty years ago. "Where did you get these?" he asked the young neighbor, his voice cracking. She explained she'd bought them from a salvage yard two counties over. Tomasz lowered himself onto a stack of lumber, still turning a board in his hands, shaking his head slowly, unable to stop staring at that crooked red letter.

My neighbor Felicity had hired the cheapest fencing outfit in town, and I wandered over with a lawn chair and a sandwich, ready to enjoy the spectacle. The truck backed in, the driver hopped out, and I nearly dropped the sandwich into the grass. It was Desmond. My Desmond, from eleventh grade, the boy who had moved to Nova Scotia without saying goodbye. He had a beard now and a tool belt, and he was squinting at the post holes like they had personally offended him. I sat frozen in the chair, mustard dripping onto my knee. Felicity waved me over to "meet the guy," and I stood up too fast and knocked the chair sideways. He looked up. I watched the recognition hit him, his hand stopping halfway to his hat. "Rosalind?" he said. My heart was thumping so hard I could feel it in my ears. Of all the backyards in all the world, I kept thinking, he had to dig post holes along mine.

Priya expected the neighbor's plans to be an act of quiet hostility. The Hendersons had barely spoken to her since the dispute over the maple tree, so when Mrs. Henderson slid a folder across the porch railing, Priya opened it with her jaw already set. Then her jaw went slack. The drawing showed a low picket fence running the length of both yards, and right in the middle, where their gardens met, an arched wooden gate with a little latch. Mrs. Henderson had drawn climbing roses on it in colored pencil. "A gate?" Priya said, looking up. "Between us?" Mrs. Henderson twisted her wedding ring and said the grandchildren wanted to play with Priya's boys without walking around the block. Priya read the note in the corner twice, "so the kids can come and go," and felt her cheeks go warm. She had prepared a speech about property rights. She had a lawyer's number on a sticky note in her pocket. She found herself folding the sticky note into a tiny square instead.

I almost threw the envelope away. It looked like every other notice from Hargreave Property Management, the same cheap gray paper, the same smudged logo, and I'd learned to expect bad news inside: rent up again, parking fees, a reminder about trash bins. I slit it open standing over the recycling bin and skimmed the first line, then stopped and read it again more slowly. The landlord was lowering my rent. Not by a little, either. By two hundred dollars a month, effective immediately, "in recognition of your care for the unit." I actually laughed out loud in the empty hallway. Then I flipped the page over to check the back for fine print, and held it up to the light like a counterfeit bill. Nothing. I read the signature. It was the owner himself, a man I'd met exactly once. I called my sister, and when she picked up I just said, "You will not believe this," and my voice was shaking.

Mrs. Adebayo-Clarke had lived in apartment 4C for twenty-two years and could recognize the landlord's handwriting from across the lobby. So when the letter appeared under her door in a crisp cream envelope with a wax seal, she frowned at it for a full minute before touching it. Wax. Nobody used wax. She slipped her reading glasses on and sat down at the kitchen table. The letter, in elaborate looping script, was an invitation. The landlord was retiring and wished to offer his longest-standing tenants the chance to buy their apartments at the price he'd paid in 1998. Her teacup stopped halfway to her lips and stayed there. She set it down without drinking, spilling some onto the tablecloth, and didn't notice. "Nineteen ninety-eight," she whispered to the empty kitchen. She pushed her glasses up, then took them off and put them back on, as if a different pair of eyes might read a different number.

Kenji was expecting an eviction notice. The pipes had burst, he'd been behind on rent twice, and his landlord, a terse woman named Ms. Valdez, had stopped returning his texts. When the certified letter came, he signed for it with a damp palm and carried it up three flights like it was radioactive. He sat on the edge of the bed and tore it open. A check fell out onto the carpet. He stared at it on the floor before picking it up. Twelve hundred dollars. The letter explained that an inspection had found the burst pipes were the building's fault, not his, and that she was refunding two months of rent for the inconvenience, along with an apology for her silence. Kenji read the word apology three times. He walked to the window, then back to the bed, then to the window again, the check pinched between two fingers, his heart racing as though he'd just run those three flights twice.

When the letter said my landlord wanted to "discuss the future of the property in person," I assumed the worst. I spent the whole weekend rehearsing arguments and looking up tenant rights. By the time I walked into the café on Monday, I had a folder of printouts and a jaw so tight it ached. Mr. Ferreira was already there, an old man with a newsboy cap, and he slid a second letter across the table toward me. It was his will. Or a page of it. I stared at the paragraph he'd highlighted and felt the floor tilt. He was leaving the building to the tenants, all six of us, as a cooperative. "You fixed my gutters," he said with a shrug, "when nobody asked." My mouth went completely dry. I opened my folder of tenant laws and then closed it again, slowly, as if putting away a weapon I'd brought to a picnic. I could hear my own pulse.

The letter was addressed to her by her full name, Marguerite Lindqvist-Obi, and nobody had used all three syllables of her surname since her divorce. She stood in the vestibule turning it over. The return address was her landlord's office, but the handwriting was strangely familiar, loopy and slanted. She opened it right there, leaning against the mailboxes. The new owner of the building, the letter explained, wanted to introduce herself to every tenant personally. At the bottom was a signature Marguerite knew instantly: her college roommate, Daphne, whom she hadn't spoken to in nineteen years. Marguerite's hand flew to her mouth. She read the name again, then looked up at the ceiling as though Daphne might be standing on the floor above. A neighbor came through the door with groceries and asked if she was all right. Marguerite just held up the letter and shook it, laughing helplessly, unable to form a single coherent sentence.

Dear Tenant, it began, and I braced for the usual. But the second paragraph made me sit down on the stairs. My landlord, a man I'd assumed didn't know which unit I lived in, wrote that he'd noticed the lights in my window on late into the night all winter and had seen me carrying textbooks in and out. He was offering to freeze my rent until I finished nursing school. I read it again, slowly, mouthing the words. Then I turned it over, half certain I'd find a demand for something on the back. Blank. "He noticed the lights?" I said out loud to no one, and my voice echoed in the stairwell. I felt my face go hot and then cold. For three years I'd thought of him as a faceless bank account number. I sat there on the cold step for ten minutes, the letter trembling in my lap, unable to decide whether to cry or to go knock on his door.

The gate agent's voice crackled over the speaker: the flight to Denver was delayed four hours. A groan rolled through the crowd, and I joined it, slumping back into the plastic seat. Then the man next to me turned, and I froze with my phone halfway to my ear. It was my high school chemistry teacher, Mr. Abernathy, the one who'd told me I'd never amount to anything if I didn't stop blowing things up. He looked older, his hair gone white, but the same bow tie sat at his throat. He squinted at me, then his eyes went wide. "Tobias Mwangi?" he said. I nodded, too startled to say anything. "You're the reason I still have a scar on my wrist," he added. I burst out laughing, an embarrassing honk that made the whole row look over. I'd spent twenty years imagining what I'd say if I ever saw him again, and here I was, speechless at Gate B14, holding a cold pretzel.

Ingrid had already resigned herself to sleeping on the airport floor. The departures board had flipped from DELAYED to CANCELED and back to DELAYED so many times she'd stopped looking. She was lying across three seats with her coat over her face when someone tapped her shoulder. She sat up to find a flight attendant holding out an envelope. "The captain asked me to give you this," the woman said. Ingrid blinked at her. Inside was a handwritten note: You helped my mother with her bags in Oslo last spring. Please accept an upgrade for the delay. Ingrid's jaw dropped. She remembered the old woman, vaguely, a tiny lady with a suitcase twice her size, but she'd never imagined anyone would remember her back. She looked up at the attendant, then down at the note, then all around the gate as if the captain might be hiding behind a pillar. "Are you serious?" she asked, and her voice cracked like a teenager's.

Six hours into the delay, Hamid had memorized every shop in Terminal C. He'd bought a neck pillow he didn't need and eaten two sad sandwiches. When the announcement came that the cause of the delay was "a VIP passenger," he rolled his eyes along with everyone else. Then the jet bridge doors opened and a small, elderly woman in a purple tracksuit shuffled through, flanked by two security guards. Hamid's eyes narrowed, then widened. He sat up so suddenly the neck pillow tumbled off his lap. It was his grandmother. His grandmother, who was supposed to be in Karachi, who had told him on the phone just last week that she was too old to travel. She spotted him across the gate and waved like a queen. Hamid stood up, sat back down, stood up again. "Nani?" he croaked. Every head in the gate area swiveled toward him. She just grinned, toothy and triumphant, as if she'd been planning this for months.

I was sure the delay would cost me the job interview. I'd been pacing near the window for an hour, rehearsing what I'd say to the hiring manager when I called to cancel, my stomach in a knot. Then a woman in a gray blazer sat down at the charging station beside me, opened her laptop, and I glimpsed my own résumé on the screen. I stopped breathing. She scrolled through it, frowning thoughtfully, then picked up her phone. A second later, my phone buzzed in my pocket. I stared at it, at her, at it again. Her eyes lifted to meet mine across the charging station, and I watched her look down at the photo on my résumé and back up at my face. "Oh my goodness," she said. "Are you Wilhelmina Ashworth?" I nodded dumbly. She laughed and closed the laptop. "Well, I suppose we're both stuck. Want to do the interview here?" My knees actually wobbled as I sat down.

Rafael was prepared for a long night: delay announcements had been stacking up since noon. What he wasn't prepared for was the pilot walking out into the gate area with a guitar. The man was still in his uniform, cap tucked under his arm, and he perched on the edge of the check-in desk, tuned up, and began to play. Rafael lowered his paperback. Around him, people were sitting up, nudging each other, pulling out phones. The pilot launched into an old bossa nova tune, one Rafael's father used to hum while shaving, and Rafael's breath snagged in his chest. He leaned forward, eyes wide, mouth slightly open. When the pilot asked if anyone knew the words to the second verse, Rafael's hand went up before he'd decided to raise it. A woman across the aisle stared at him. He stared back, just as startled at himself, and then he was singing, in a crowded airport, in front of a hundred strangers.

The text arrived at the exact moment the board flashed DELAYED: Turn around. I frowned, assuming it was a scam, and glanced back anyway. My husband was standing at the end of the concourse holding a paper bag from my favorite bakery. My husband, who was supposed to be at home with the twins three hundred miles away. My suitcase handle slipped out of my fingers and the bag tipped over with a clatter. I didn't even pick it up. "What are you doing here?" I called, much too loudly, and a businessman flinched. Bashir walked toward me with a sheepish grin and explained that he'd seen the storm warnings, booked the same flight to keep me company, and that his mother had the kids. I kept shaking my head as he talked, a slow incredulous shake, my hand pressed flat against my chest. Eleven years of marriage and I'd never once seen him book anything spontaneously in his life.

The doctor came in smiling, which threw me off from the start. I'd spent the whole week convinced the lump was cancer. I'd written letters to my kids. I'd even looked up the price of wigs. So when Dr. Hassan sat down, crossed her legs, and said "It's a lipoma, completely benign," I just stared at her. My brain couldn't hold the word benign. It kept sliding off. "Benign," I repeated stupidly. She nodded and started explaining fat cells and harmless growths, and I didn't hear a single sentence. I was looking at the poster on the wall behind her, a cartoon of a kidney, and thinking about the letters in my desk drawer. My hands were trembling on my knees. When she asked if I had any questions, I opened my mouth and the only thing that came out was a startled little laugh. She tilted her head at me, and I laughed again, louder, and then I couldn't stop.

Gwendolyn had been coming to the clinic for routine bloodwork every year since she turned sixty. She barely listened anymore. So when the nurse practitioner looked up from the screen and said, "Well, this is interesting," Gwendolyn glanced up from her crossword with mild irritation. "Your cholesterol," the nurse continued, "is the best I've seen on any patient over seventy." Gwendolyn's pen stopped in mid-letter. For a decade she'd been scolded about that number, lectured about butter and bacon and the dangers of her Sunday fry-ups. "The best?" she repeated, and her voice rose into a squeak she hadn't made since girlhood. The nurse turned the screen so she could see. Gwendolyn leaned closer, squinting through her bifocals, then leaned back, then forward again. She wrote the number in the margin of her crossword so she could show her daughter. She tapped the pen on her knee and kept murmuring "Well, I never" under her breath as she gathered her coat.

I'd only done the DNA test as a joke, a birthday present from my roommate. Then the genetic counselor called and asked if I could come in, and I spent two days imagining terrible inherited diseases. Sitting in her office, I bit the inside of my cheek until it hurt. She folded her hands and told me I didn't carry anything dangerous. Then she paused. "But the results show something else you should know," she said gently. "You have a full sibling in the database. A brother." I blinked at her. I was an only child. I had always been an only child. My parents had told me so every single day of my life, and I had believed them the way you believe in gravity. "That's a mistake," I said, my voice flat and odd. She shook her head and slid a printout across the desk. His name was Matteo. He lived forty minutes away. My ears were ringing, and my fingers wouldn't close around the paper.

Dmitri had come in for a sprained ankle. That was all. He'd rolled it stepping off a curb, and his wife had insisted on an X-ray. He sat on the crinkly paper of the exam table, swinging his good foot, when the radiologist walked in holding the film up to the light. "Mr. Volkov," she said, "did you know you have a needle in your foot?" Dmitri stopped swinging. "A what?" She pointed. There it was on the ghostly gray image, a thin bright line lodged between two bones. He leaned forward, then back, staring at his own foot as though it belonged to a stranger. And then the memory came crashing in: age six, his grandmother's sewing room, a dropped pin, a scream, nobody ever finding it. "Forty years," he muttered. "It's been in there forty years." He started to laugh, rubbing his ankle, while the radiologist watched him with raised eyebrows.

The cardiologist had a habit of clicking her pen, and I counted twelve clicks before she spoke. I'd had the palpitations for months. I'd stopped drinking coffee. I'd quit running. I'd made my peace. "Your heart is fine," she said. "It's your thyroid." I sat very still. Then I asked her to say it again, and she did, more slowly, and drew a little butterfly shape on her notepad to show me where it was. A pill a day, she said. That's all. I looked down at my sneakers, which I hadn't worn for running since spring, and felt a strange lurch, like missing a step on the stairs. All those nights lying awake feeling my chest thud. All those plans I'd quietly abandoned. "A pill," I said. She nodded. I picked up the drawing of the butterfly and stared at it, holding it with both hands as though it might fly off, and found I was grinning so wide my cheeks hurt.

Yusuf's mother had been in remission for two years, and the scan was meant to be a formality. He drove her to the appointment, chatting about the weather, his mind on a work email. When the oncologist walked in with a colleague trailing behind her, Yusuf straightened in his chair. Two doctors meant news. But the oncologist was beaming. "We wanted to show you something," she said, and pulled up an image. The old tumor site was simply gone, not shrunken, not stable, but gone, a clean dark space where the shadow used to be. "We almost never see a scan this clear," the second doctor added, almost reverently. Yusuf's mother gripped his arm so hard her fingernails dug in. He turned to look at her and found her mouth open, her eyes huge behind her glasses. Neither of them spoke. Yusuf could hear the hum of the fluorescent lights and his own breath, which seemed to have stopped for a moment altogether.

The red number at the top of the page was 97. I looked at it, then flipped the paper over to make sure Ms. Okonkwo hadn't handed me someone else's test by mistake. My name was there, in my own messy handwriting. I flipped it back. Still 97. This was the calculus exam I'd walked out of absolutely certain I'd failed, the one where I'd guessed on the last three problems and spent the bus ride home drafting an apology to my parents. I could feel my face heating up. Beside me, my friend Lucía leaned over and whispered, "What'd you get?" and I just tilted the page toward her without a word. Her eyebrows rocketed upward. "Shut up," she hissed. I couldn't stop staring at it, rubbing my thumb over the red ink as if it might smudge into a different number. Under it, Ms. Okonkwo had written: I knew you had it in you.

Benedikt had never gotten anything higher than a C in English. He accepted it the way he accepted being short: a fact of life. So when Mr. Achterberg paused at his desk, held the essay out, and said, "Stay after class, please," Benedikt's stomach dropped. He assumed plagiarism, or worse. When the room emptied, the teacher sat on the edge of the desk next to him. "I'd like to submit this to the regional writing competition," he said. "With your permission." Benedikt looked down at the paper. A in the corner, circled twice. Comments all down the margin, mostly exclamation points. He read one: This line made me put my pen down. He felt his ears burning. "Mine?" he asked, pointing at his own chest like an idiot. The teacher nodded. Benedikt picked up the essay and held it very carefully, by the edges, the way you'd hold a photograph of someone you'd lost. His voice, when he finally said yes, came out as a croak.

I knew the exam had gone badly. What I wasn't ready for was the blank page. Professor Lindgren dropped it on my desk face down, and when I turned it over there was no grade, no comments, just a yellow sticky note: Please see me. I went cold. In her office she held up my answer sheet next to another student's, and they were identical, word for word, down to a misspelled "hypothesis." My mouth fell open. "I didn't," I stammered, "I would never," and then I saw the other name at the top. It was my twin brother, Ezekiel, who wasn't even in this class. He was enrolled in the night section. Somehow the department had mixed our scantrons and essays together in the scanner. The professor watched my face go from white to red to something in between. "So you're telling me there are two of you?" she said slowly. I could only nod, gripping the arms of the chair.

Sung-min's hands always shook on test-return days, so she sat on them. The chemistry teacher went down the rows slowly, tapping each paper onto each desk, and when he reached hers he didn't put it down. He held it up for the whole class to see. Sung-min wanted to sink through the floor. Then he said, "This is the first perfect score I've given in fourteen years of teaching." The room went silent. Somebody in the back let out a low whistle. Sung-min's head snapped up. She looked at the paper in his hand, at the big red 100 on it, and then at her classmates, who were all turning around in their seats to look at her. Her cheeks flamed. She opened her mouth to say something but nothing came out, just a little squeak. When he finally set the test down in front of her, she touched the edge of it with one finger, as though checking whether it was actually real.

The history final came back with a giant red question mark scrawled across the first page. That was it. No grade. I stared at it, and then I noticed the note at the bottom in my teacher's tiny cramped print: Where did you learn this? I flipped through. I'd written about my great-grandfather's village in Gujarat, about the partition, using stories my grandmother told me while braiding my hair. I thought I'd been lazy, padding the essay with family anecdotes because I hadn't studied. After class, Mr. Pemberton asked if my grandmother would be willing to be interviewed for the university's oral history archive. "Nobody has documented that village," he said, leaning forward, eyes bright. "Nobody." I blinked at him for a long, long moment. "My Ba?" I finally said, and my voice wobbled. I pictured her in her armchair with the TV on too loud, and could not, for the life of me, picture her in an archive.

Ozzie had already told his mother he'd failed. He'd said it at breakfast, staring into his cereal, to get it over with. So when Mrs. Castellanos placed the algebra test on his desk, he didn't even look at it right away. He looked out the window at the parking lot and thought about summer school. Then the kid behind him, Jaylen, poked him in the back. "Dude. Look at it." Ozzie looked. A big green B-plus sat in the corner, with a smiley face. He actually flinched backward in his chair. He pulled the paper closer, then held it at arm's length, then turned it over, checking for the catch. Every single problem had his own scrawled work beside it, and most of them had check marks. He'd been so sure. He'd felt the failure in his gut. Ozzie sat there with his mouth open, already wondering how on earth he was going to explain this to his mother after the speech he'd made over the cereal.

I was reaching for the last carton of oat milk when another hand closed on it at the same moment. I turned, ready to be polite about it, and the words died in my throat. Freckles. A gap between the front teeth. A chipped silver ring on the thumb. "Odalys?" I said, and it came out as barely a whisper. She dropped her basket. Apples went rolling under the yogurt case and neither of us moved to get them. The last time I'd seen her we were nineteen, crying at a bus station in Miami, promising to write every week. We'd managed about three months. Now here she was in a supermarket in Minneapolis, in a parka, holding the same carton of milk as me. "You live here?" she asked, her eyes enormous. "Since when?" "Since forever," I said, laughing in a high, breathless way that didn't sound like me. A stock boy edged past us, gathering apples, and we just stood there, gawking at each other like idiots.

Leopold was squeezing avocados with the grim concentration of a man who had been burned before when someone behind him said, "Still doing it wrong, I see." He spun around so fast he knocked a pyramid of limes onto the floor. The man grinning at him was older, heavier, bald now, but the laugh was exactly the same. Augustin. His best friend from the seminary, the one who'd left in the middle of the night forty years ago and never sent so much as a postcard. Leopold's hands went limp at his sides. An avocado slipped from his fingers and thudded onto his shoe. "You're supposed to be in Argentina," he said, which was the only thing his brain could produce. "I was," Augustin said. "For thirty-eight years." Leopold stared at him, then at the limes rolling across the tiles, then at him again. He opened his mouth and closed it twice. A woman with a cart had to steer around them both, tutting, and Leopold didn't even notice her.

The checkout line was crawling, so I was scrolling my phone and not paying attention when the cashier said, "Paper or plastic, Bea?" Nobody calls me Bea anymore. I looked up. The name tag said Corinne, but I'd have known that face anywhere: the sharp chin, the one eyebrow that always arched higher than the other. Corinne, who had been my lab partner, my bridesmaid, and then, after one terrible argument, nobody at all for twelve years. I forgot what I was holding. My credit card slid off the counter and fell between the conveyor belt and the register. "Corinne," I said, and my voice cracked. She was blushing, scanning a box of cereal with exaggerated care, her hands not quite steady. "I moved back," she said. "Last month." I bent down to fish out my card and nearly banged my head on the counter coming back up. The man behind me cleared his throat impatiently. Neither of us paid him any attention whatsoever.

Nadia had only stopped at the store for cough drops. She was standing in the pharmacy aisle reading labels when a small child came barreling around the corner and slammed into her knees, followed by a woman calling, "Theo, slow down!" Nadia looked up, and the woman looked at her, and both of them stopped dead. "Nadia Haddad?" the woman breathed. "Ruth?" Nadia said, gaping. Ruth Feldman, her roommate from graduate school, the one who'd sworn up and down that she would never, ever have children. And here was a toddler clinging to Ruth's leg, wearing a dinosaur raincoat, with Ruth's exact frown. Nadia looked from the child to Ruth and back again, her cough drops forgotten in her hand. "Is he yours?" Ruth laughed, slightly embarrassed, and said there were two more at home. Nadia's eyebrows rose so far she could feel them. "Three?" she said. "Ruth. Three?" The toddler stared up at her solemnly while Nadia shook her head in disbelief.

I nearly walked right past him. He was standing in front of the cereal, a huge bearded man in a construction vest, and I only glanced over because he was humming. Humming the school fight song, of all things, badly off-key. I stopped so abruptly my cart rolled on without me and bumped into a display of crackers. "Marcus Oyelaran," I said, and he turned, and his face went through about four expressions in two seconds. Last time I saw him he was a skinny kid in braces who couldn't lift a backpack without groaning. "No way," he said. "Kwame? Little Kwame?" Little. I'm six foot two. I started laughing so hard I had to grab a shelf. He dropped the box of cereal in his hand and wrapped me in a hug that lifted my feet clean off the floor. When he set me down I was still blinking at him, trying to find the skinny kid somewhere under all that beard.

Solveig was on her knees on the floor of the frozen aisle, digging for the last bag of peas at the back of the freezer, when a voice above her said, "Solveig Brandt, as I live and breathe." She jerked her head up and cracked it on the freezer shelf. Rubbing the bump, she squinted up into the fluorescent lights. Standing there was Mrs. Okafor-Reyes, who had lived next door to her family in Bergen when Solveig was six, the woman who had taught her to bake bread and then vanished when her family emigrated. "How?" was all Solveig could say. "How are you here?" The old woman laughed and explained she'd moved to be near her son. Solveig sat back on her heels in the freezer aisle, cold air rolling over her, the peas forgotten. She kept saying "how" over and over, like a broken record, while Mrs. Okafor-Reyes held out her hand to help her up off the floor.

The engine coughed twice on the highway and then simply stopped. I coasted onto the shoulder, gripping the wheel, already doing the mental math: tow truck, missed meeting, angry boss. I popped the hood and stood staring into it as if I knew what I was looking at. Then a car pulled in behind me, and out stepped my boss. Ms. Takahashi, in her pressed charcoal suit, rolling up her sleeves. I actually took a step back and bumped into my own car. "You know engines?" I blurted. "My father was a mechanic," she said, already leaning over the battery. I had worked for this woman for six years. I had never seen her touch anything dirtier than a fountain pen. She fiddled with a cable, told me to try the ignition, and the car roared to life. I sat behind the wheel with my mouth hanging open while she wiped her hands on a handkerchief, looking completely pleased with herself.

Cormac was halfway across the bridge when the dashboard lit up like a Christmas tree and the car shuddered to a stop. Horns blared behind him. He flicked on his hazards, cursed, and climbed out into the drizzle. That was when he noticed the smell. Not smoke. Cinnamon. He walked around to the back of the car and found the trunk had popped open in the jolt, and inside, where he expected his gym bag and jumper cables, sat a large white cake box tied with ribbon. He stared at it. He hadn't put it there. He lifted the lid with one finger. Happy Anniversary, Cormac, piped in blue icing. He stood frozen in the rain, cars swerving around him, a slow heat spreading up his neck. His anniversary. Today. He had completely forgotten, and his wife had hidden a cake in his car. His phone buzzed. He answered, and before she could speak, he heard himself say, "How did you even get the trunk open?"

Smoke started curling out from under the hood just after the gas station. I pulled over, heart hammering, and called a tow truck, then sat on the guardrail and waited. Forty minutes later, a battered yellow truck crunched onto the gravel, and the driver hopped down. She was maybe seventy, with a long silver braid and a cardigan, and she was wearing pink rubber gloves. I stood up, then sat back down. "You're the tow truck?" I asked. "Fifty-two years," she said cheerfully, hooking the chains under my bumper with the speed of someone half her age. I watched with my hands in my pockets, completely unable to stop gawking. She diagnosed a cracked radiator hose just by sniffing. She told me a story about towing a governor's limousine in 1979. She asked if I wanted to ride up front, and offered me a peppermint. I climbed into the cab and spent the whole drive turned sideways in my seat, staring at her, utterly delighted.

Fatima's car died at a red light, in the middle of the busiest intersection in town, at eight-fifteen in the morning. She sat there with her head on the steering wheel, listening to the horns, waiting for the humiliation to be over. A tap on the window made her lift her head. A young man in a suit was standing there, and behind him, five more people from the cars around her, all of them already pushing. Pushing. The car began to roll. Fatima sat bolt upright, her hands flying off the wheel and then back to it, steering wildly toward the curb. "What is happening?" she said aloud to no one. Nobody she knew. Strangers in office clothes, a woman in heels, a teenager with a skateboard under one arm. They got her to the curb, waved, and climbed back into their own cars as the light turned green. Fatima sat there with the engine silent, her hand over her mouth, watching them drive away.

The car had been making a clunking sound for a week, and I'd ignored it, and now it had died in the parking lot of a diner forty miles from my office. I went inside to use the phone, since mine was dead too, because of course it was. The waitress came over with a coffee pot, glanced at me, and froze. The coffee pot tilted dangerously. "Hollis?" she said. I squinted at her name tag: Imogen. My little sister's best friend, who'd babysat me when I was ten. She'd moved away after high school and no one had heard from her since. My fingers went numb around the menu. "You work here?" I said stupidly. "I own it," she said, and grinned. I glanced out the window at my car, steaming gently in the lot, and then back at her, my jaw loose. Fifteen years. One bad radiator. I laughed so suddenly I spilled the water glass she'd just set down.

When Agnieszka's car rolled to a halt on the country road, there was no cell signal, no houses in sight, and nothing but corn in every direction. She got out and kicked a tire for good measure. Then she heard the hoofbeats. Around the bend came a horse-drawn buggy, driven by a boy no older than twelve in a broad-brimmed hat. He pulled up beside her and asked politely if she needed help. Agnieszka blinked at him, then at the horse, then at her useless car. Before she could say anything, the boy hopped down, rummaged in her engine with total confidence, and tightened something with a wrench he pulled from his pocket. "Try it now," he said. She turned the key. The engine caught. Agnieszka leaned out the window, staring at him in utter bewilderment. "How do you know engines?" she asked. He shrugged. "My uncle fixes tractors," he said, climbed back into his buggy, and clicked his tongue at the horse.

It was 1:40 in the morning and I was sitting at the kitchen table with my phone face up in front of me, rehearsing the lecture. Curfew was midnight. Midnight. I'd typed out three texts and deleted them all. When I finally heard the key in the lock, I stood up, arms folded, ready. The door opened, and my daughter Zainab walked in carrying a bakery box, flour streaked across her cheek. Behind her came old Mr. Petrakis from next door, also covered in flour. My arms dropped. "His oven broke," Zainab said, "and he had the church bake sale tomorrow, so we used his sister's oven across town." Mr. Petrakis held up a tray of baklava like an offering. I just stood there in my bathrobe, my entire lecture evaporating. My mouth opened and nothing came out. Zainab set the box down and kissed my cheek. "You look like you've seen a ghost, Mom," she said, and I sat down hard in the chair.

Every car that passed the house made Theodora's head jerk toward the window. Her son Rory was ninety minutes late and not answering his phone, and she'd already called two of his friends' parents, who were sleepy and unhelpful. When headlights finally swung into the driveway, she flung open the front door and marched out in her slippers. Then she stopped dead on the porch step. It wasn't Rory's battered hatchback. It was a police cruiser. Her knees went weak. The officer got out, opened the back door, and Rory climbed out holding a small, shivering puppy wrapped in his jacket. The officer was smiling. "Your son stopped traffic on Route 9 to rescue this little guy," she said. "Wanted to make sure he got home safe." Theodora gripped the porch railing with both hands. Her heart, which had been pounding with fear, now pounded with something else entirely. She stared at the puppy, then at her son, and could not find a single word.

The plan had been simple: wait up, lights off, catch him sneaking in through the basement window like I did at his age. I'd been sitting in the dark on the basement stairs for an hour, feeling smug. At 12:30 the window creaked open. A pair of sneakers appeared. Then a second pair. Then a third. My smugness drained away. Three teenagers tumbled onto the old couch, and the last one through was my own mother, seventy-four years old, in a tracksuit, laughing. I flicked on the light. All four of them froze like raccoons. "Mom?" I said. My voice came out as a squeak. My son Ignatius, hair full of leaves, looked at his grandmother, who looked right back at me without a shred of guilt. "We went to see the meteor shower," she said. "He drove. I navigated." I stood on the stairs with my hand still on the switch, my brain refusing to arrange what I was seeing into anything that made sense.

Ravi had assumed his daughter would come home late, apologetic, and smelling faintly of somebody else's cigarettes. That was how these nights usually went. So when the door opened at eleven fifty-nine, exactly one minute before curfew, he glanced at the clock twice. Then Meera walked in holding a trophy nearly as tall as her torso. Ravi's book slid off his lap. "What is that?" he asked. "Regional debate championship," she said, setting it on the coffee table. "I didn't tell you I'd entered. I didn't want you to come and watch me lose." Ravi leaned forward and read the engraved plaque, then read it again, his lips moving. First place. His daughter, who mumbled at the dinner table, who wouldn't order her own food at restaurants. He looked up at her, then back at the trophy, his eyebrows climbing steadily toward his hairline. "You argued?" he said finally. "In front of people? On purpose?" Meera rolled her eyes and went upstairs, grinning.

I heard the car before I saw it. Not my son's rattling sedan, but something low and smooth that purred. I got up from the armchair, peeked through the blinds, and nearly pulled them off the window. A white stretch limousine was idling at the curb. The back door opened and out climbed Jonah, my quiet, gangly sixteen-year-old, in his rumpled Saturday clothes, waving goodbye to someone inside. The limo pulled away. I was at the front door before he could knock, holding it open, my bathrobe gaping, my hair sticking up. "Whose car was that?" I demanded, too loudly. Jonah blinked. "Oh. Mr. Kowalczyk. From the chess club tournament. He's, um, a retired tech guy. He gave everybody rides home." I looked out at the empty street where the limousine had been, then back at my son. "A limousine," I repeated. He nodded and walked past me toward the fridge. I stood in the doorway for a full minute, staring at the street.

It was past two when Lucinda finally heard footsteps on the porch, and she was halfway through a furious sentence before she saw her son's face. He was crying. Not sniffling, but really crying, the way he hadn't since he was small. Her anger evaporated mid-word. Then she saw what he was holding: a crumpled piece of paper. "I got in," Esteban said. "Juilliard. They emailed tonight, and I was at Danny's, and I just, I had to walk around for a while." Lucinda grabbed the doorframe. Juilliard. He'd told her he hadn't even applied. He'd told her it was pointless, that kids like him didn't get into places like that, and she had believed him and quietly mourned it. "You applied?" she whispered. He nodded. She snatched the paper from his hand and read it under the porch light, holding it so close to her face that her nose nearly touched it, her breath coming in quick, ragged gasps.

When my manager's assistant said, "Mr. Bergström would like to see you, now," I felt every eye in the open-plan office swivel toward me. I walked the long carpet to his office like a man walking the plank, running through every mistake I'd made that quarter. The door was closed. I knocked, and a voice called, "Come in." I pushed it open and stopped in the doorway. The room was full of balloons. Actual balloons, dozens of them, blue and silver, bobbing against the ceiling. Mr. Bergström, who I had never once seen smile, was standing behind his desk in a paper party hat. "Twenty years, Ansel," he said. "Did you think we'd forget?" I had forgotten. I genuinely had. My hand went to my chest. Behind me, I heard my coworkers crowding the doorway, giggling. I turned around and stared at them, then back at the balloons, then at the party hat, completely unable to form a sentence.

Chiamaka was sure she was being fired. Her numbers had been down, and the regional director had been in meetings with the manager all week, the blinds drawn. When she was finally summoned, she gathered her bag and her coat, figuring she wouldn't be coming back to her desk. Ms. Ridley gestured for her to sit, folded her hands, and said, "I'm resigning." Chiamaka's coat slid off her lap onto the floor. "And I've recommended you to replace me," Ms. Ridley added. Chiamaka stared at her. She was aware, distantly, of her coat on the carpet and her bag on her shoulder and the fact that her mouth was open. "Me?" she said. "But my numbers..." "Your numbers were down because you took on everyone else's problem accounts," Ms. Ridley said. "We noticed." Chiamaka bent to pick up her coat and missed it on the first grab. Her fingers were trembling. She sat back up holding it in a crumpled heap against her chest.

I'd only worked at the bakery for three weeks, and when the manager called me into her cramped back office, I assumed I'd burned one too many baguettes. She pointed to a chair, closed the door, and set a laptop on the desk between us. "I need to show you something," she said, and pressed play. It was security footage from the night before: me, after closing, giving the unsold bread to the man who slept in the doorway across the street. I felt my face go white. I'd broken the rule, the one about wasted product. "I'm sorry," I started, but she held up a hand. "The owner saw this," she said. "He wants to start a program. Daily donations. He wants you to run it." I sat back in the chair like I'd been pushed. "Run it?" I said. I looked at the frozen image on the screen, at my own small figure handing over a paper bag, and couldn't stop blinking.

Wendell had been called into the manager's office exactly twice in his thirty-year career at the plant, and both times somebody had died. So when the foreman jerked his head toward the stairs, Wendell's stomach dropped through his boots. He climbed to the glass office slowly, gripping the rail. Inside, the manager, a young fellow named Pradeep who still wore sneakers to work, was sitting on the floor surrounded by cardboard boxes. "Close the door," Pradeep said. "I need your help. The company's selling the plant." Wendell's hand stopped on the doorknob. "To the employees," Pradeep went on, grinning. "If enough of us buy in, we'd own it. I want you on the board." Wendell lowered himself onto a box because his legs had gone soft. The plant. Thirty years of clocking in, and now someone wanted to give him a piece of it. He took his cap off, turned it around in his hands, put it back on, and took it off again.

The email just said "My office, 3 p.m." and nothing else. I spent the whole afternoon refreshing it, as if more words might appear. At three I knocked on Ms. Kaczmarek's door, and she waved me in without looking up from her screen. Then she swiveled her monitor around. On it was a photo of a painting, a watercolor of a lighthouse. My watercolor. The one I'd posted anonymously online at two in the morning, under a fake name, to an account nobody followed. "Is this yours?" she asked. My face burned. I couldn't even speak. I just nodded. "My wife bought a print of it," she said. "It's hanging in our kitchen. I recognized the coffee stain in the corner. You do that on your reports, too." I stared at her. Then I laughed, a nervous yelp, and covered my mouth. Somewhere out there, my lighthouse was hanging in my boss's kitchen, coffee stain and all.

Itzel stood outside the manager's door for a full minute before knocking, smoothing her uniform and rehearsing her apology for the broken espresso machine. When she finally stepped inside, the manager wasn't alone. Sitting beside him, in a crisp suit, was an older woman with Itzel's own dark eyes and stubborn chin. Itzel stopped halfway to the chair. Her breath caught. "Tía Paloma?" she said. Her aunt, who'd left the family in Oaxaca when Itzel was a baby, who was a name mentioned only in lowered voices at Christmas. The woman rose, her hands pressed together. "I own this franchise," she said quietly. "I saw your name on the payroll last month. I've been trying to work up the courage." Itzel's hand found the back of the chair and held on. The manager, looking deeply uncomfortable, mumbled something and slipped out. Itzel didn't hear him go. She was staring at her aunt's face, searching it, unable to believe it was really there.

I was only up in the attic to find the Christmas lights. I shifted a box marked TAXES 1987, and an envelope slid out from between two folders and landed on my sneaker. It was addressed to me. To me, in my own name, in handwriting I didn't recognize, postmarked from Lisbon in 1994. Unopened. I sat down on a rolled-up rug, dust rising around me, and turned it over and over. I was eleven in 1994. Who in Lisbon knew I existed? I slid my finger under the flap. Inside was a single sheet of blue paper and a photograph of a young man holding a baby. Me. The baby was me. The letter began: My dearest Cristiano, your mother says I am not to write, but I am your father. I read that line four times. The attic was stifling, but a cold prickle ran down my arms. Downstairs I could hear my mother humming in the kitchen, and I couldn't move.

Harriet had promised her daughter she'd finally clear out the attic, and she'd been making good progress through boxes of old curtains and broken lamps when she found the hatbox. Inside, wrapped in tissue paper, was a bundle of letters tied with a faded green ribbon. She expected her mother's love letters from her father. She untied the ribbon, unfolded the first one, and blinked. The letters were from her father, yes, but addressed to someone named Clement. My dearest Clement, the first line read. Harriet sat back heavily against a dusty trunk. She read the next letter, and the next, her eyes racing down the pages, her lips parted. Her quiet, pipe-smoking father, who had fixed clocks and sung in the church choir, had loved someone she'd never heard of, for years, in secret. "Oh, Daddy," she breathed. She held a letter up to the dim bulb as though the light might explain it, and her hand would not stop trembling.

The attic smelled of mothballs and old rain. I was hauling out a broken rocking horse when I spotted a yellowed envelope wedged under the floorboard by the chimney, as if someone had hidden it on purpose. The address was in a child's careful print: To whoever lives here in the future. I laughed out loud, startled, and pried it free. The letter inside was dated 1961. Hello future person, it said. My name is Douglas and I am nine. I hope you have flying cars. I sat down right there on the dusty planks, cross-legged, and kept reading. Douglas described his dog, his little sister, his hatred of turnips. At the bottom he'd drawn a map with an X and the words: treasure under the third step. I stared at the map. My heart was suddenly pounding like I was nine myself. I scrambled down the ladder so fast I scraped my shin, heading straight for the porch steps.

Mihail found the letter tucked inside a copy of Anna Karenina, which was inside a crate of his late uncle's books, which was buried under thirty years of attic junk. He nearly missed it. He flipped the book open to check for a bookmark, and an envelope fluttered out onto his knee. It was addressed to him. Not to his uncle, to Mihail, in his uncle's spidery script, with the words: Open when you find this, nephew. You will be grown. Mihail stopped breathing for a moment. His uncle had died when he was fourteen. He'd always assumed nobody in the family had ever paid him much mind. He opened it with clumsy fingers. Inside was a single page and a small brass key. The letter explained that the key opened a safety deposit box in a bank in Bucharest. Mihail held the key up in a beam of dusty light, turning it slowly, his eyebrows drawn together, his mouth hanging slightly open.

I was clearing the attic before we sold the house, and I'd developed a rhythm: open box, glance inside, toss into donation pile. I almost tossed the shoebox of letters too. Then I saw the stamp. It was a royal crest. I fished out the top envelope and saw that it was addressed to my grandmother, in a handsome, slanting hand, from Buckingham Palace. I sat down on the nearest box, which promptly caved in beneath me. Sprawled in the crushed cardboard, I unfolded the letter. It was a thank-you note, signed by a lady-in-waiting, for my grandmother's service as a codebreaker during the war. A codebreaker. My grandmother, who did crosswords in pen and once told me she spent the war "doing typing." I lay there on the collapsed box, laughing in short, breathless bursts, the letter held above my face. "Typing," I said aloud to the rafters. "Typing, Nana?"

Grace was looking for her old prom dress to lend to her niece when she found the letter pinned inside the garment bag. It was in her own handwriting. Teenage handwriting, rounder and bubblier, with hearts dotting the i's. Dear Grace at forty, it said. She sank onto the dusty attic floor. She had no memory of writing it. None at all. She read on, her cheeks growing warm: I hope you married Tyrone. I hope you live in Paris. I hope you are a famous architect. Grace laughed, a short startled sound, and covered her mouth. She had not married Tyrone. She lived in Ohio. She was a dental hygienist. But the last line made her catch her breath: Whatever you are, I hope you still sing in the car. She stared at the line for a long moment. She did. Every single morning, at the top of her lungs. She hadn't known it was something she'd once hoped for.

The guests were due at seven, and at six-forty I opened the oven to baste the lamb and found it stone cold. The oven light was on. The dial was turned to 400. But the lamb was pink and raw and cool to the touch, sitting there exactly the way I'd put it in two hours earlier. I just stood with the oven door open, the baster dripping onto my socks, staring. Two hours. I'd been dicing and stirring and sipping wine and humming, and the whole time the oven had been quietly doing nothing at all. I touched the rack, then the wall of the oven, then the lamb again, as if the third poke might change something. "You're kidding," I said to it. "You are actually kidding me." The doorbell rang. I jumped so hard I dropped the baster, and it skittered under the fridge. I looked at the clock, then at the door, then at the raw lamb.

Beatriz had been cooking for her future in-laws since noon. The paella was simmering, the flan was chilling, and she was wiping down the counter one last time when the doorbell rang twenty minutes early. She opened the door wiping her hands on her apron and froze. Her fiancé's mother stood on the step, smiling, holding up a battered recipe card. Beatriz recognized the handwriting at once. It was her own grandmother's. "My mother learned this from a woman in Valencia in 1962," the older woman said. "A woman named Consuelo Iglesias." Beatriz's hand slid off the doorknob. "That's my abuela," she whispered. The two women stared at each other across the threshold. The smell of saffron drifted out past them into the night. Beatriz took the card with fingers that didn't feel like her own and read the familiar slanting letters, and a small, disbelieving laugh escaped her. From inside, the timer began to beep, and she didn't move.

I'd planned the dinner party for weeks: a curry I'd been perfecting, rice with saffron, a mango cheesecake. The table was set, the candles lit, and I was stirring the pot one last time when my phone buzzed with a text from my friend Ines. Can't wait! Btw who else is coming? I texted back the guest list. Six names. Her reply came instantly: Wait. You invited Oskar AND Philippa? I frowned. Why wouldn't I? Then: They got married last weekend. Secretly. Nobody knows. I dropped the wooden spoon into the curry. It sank. I fished it out with my fingers, burning myself, and sucked on my knuckle, staring at the phone. Oskar and Philippa. Who had, as far as I knew, met exactly once, at my birthday, and argued about cheese for an hour. I read the text again. And again. The doorbell rang. Through the frosted glass I could see two figures standing very close together, holding hands.

Chef Bartholomew had cooked for presidents. A dinner for eight in his own home was nothing. He was plating the starter, tiny towers of beet and goat cheese, when his eight-year-old granddaughter Wren tugged his sleeve. "I made dessert," she said. He smiled indulgently and turned to look, expecting a bowl of melted ice cream. Instead, on the counter sat a perfect soufflé, tall and golden, quivering slightly. Bartholomew set down his tweezers very slowly. He bent close, his nose almost touching the rim. The rise was even. The top was cracked in just the right place. He looked at Wren, then at the soufflé, then at Wren again. "Who helped you?" he asked. "Nobody," she said. "I watched you on the video Mom has." The doorbell rang, guests arriving, and Bartholomew didn't hear it. He was crouched at eye level with the soufflé, his chef's whites dusted with beet juice, muttering, "Forty years. Forty years it took me."

I'd been dreading the dinner because Tamsin was bringing her new boyfriend, and she'd warned me he was "very particular about food." I'd spent the afternoon nervously making the most inoffensive meal I could think of: roast chicken, potatoes, green beans. When the doorbell rang, I smoothed my apron, opened the door, and the tray of hors d'oeuvres in my hands tilted sideways. Standing beside Tamsin was the food critic from the city paper. The same man who'd given my restaurant one star three years ago and essentially closed it. I knew his face from the photo I'd thrown darts at. He recognized me at the exact same moment. His smile faltered. "Oh," he said. "Oh dear." Tamsin looked between us, baffled. My ears were ringing. A cracker slid off the tray and landed on the doormat. I stared at him, he stared at me, and then, quite without meaning to, I started laughing, and couldn't stop.

Lorenzo was sweating over a tray of arancini when he realized the kitchen was quiet. Too quiet. His partner, Felipe, had been chopping herbs a moment ago. Lorenzo turned around, knife in hand, and saw Felipe kneeling on the tile in the middle of the kitchen, holding up a small velvet box. Lorenzo blinked. The knife clattered onto the cutting board. "You're doing this now?" he squeaked. "The guests are coming in ten minutes!" "That's why," Felipe said. "They're all in on it. They're parked down the street." Lorenzo pressed both floury hands to his cheeks, leaving white handprints, and stared down at the open box. The ring glinted under the stove light. The arancini sizzled in the pan behind him, starting to burn, and he did not even smell it. He kept looking from the ring to Felipe's nervous face and back again, his mouth opening and closing, as the smoke alarm began to shriek.

The moving truck had barely pulled away when I realized the key didn't fit. I stood in the hallway of my new building in Chicago, surrounded by boxes, jiggling the key in the lock of 5B. Nothing. I tried it upside down. Nothing. I was about to call the leasing office in tears when the door swung open from the inside. A woman in a bathrobe stood there holding a mug. Behind her I could see furniture, plants, a cat on the windowsill. "Can I help you?" she asked. I held up my lease, speechless, and she squinted at it. "Oh," she said. "That's 5B in the other building. Across the courtyard." I looked out the hall window at the identical brick tower opposite and felt my cheeks catch fire. Then I looked back at her and realized she was wearing my college sweatshirt. Same school. Same year, printed on the sleeve. "Hang on," she said slowly. "Are you Aditi?"

Henrik's new apartment in Lisbon was supposed to be a modest one-bedroom. That's what the listing said, and that's what he'd paid for. So when the landlord unlocked the door and stepped aside, Henrik took one step in and stopped. The room was enormous. Ceilings that soared up into shadowy wooden beams, tall windows thrown open to a view of the river, and a grand piano, an actual grand piano, sitting in the corner under a dust sheet. He set down his suitcase without looking at where it landed. "I think there's been a mistake," he said. The landlord laughed and shook his head. "The previous tenant left it. He said whoever came next should have it." Henrik walked over to the piano slowly, lifted the dust sheet, and ran his fingers over the keys. One note rang out in the empty room. He stood there, blinking up at the beams, unable to stop shaking his head.

My first night in Seoul, I couldn't sleep, so I went up to the rooftop of my new building to look at the city. I expected an empty concrete slab. Instead, I pushed open the heavy door and found a garden. Rows and rows of vegetables in wooden planters, strings of paper lanterns, and about fifteen elderly people sitting on folding chairs, eating watermelon at midnight. Every single one of them turned to look at me. I froze in the doorway, still in my pajamas, my hand on the door. An old woman with a straw hat waved me over and pushed a slice of watermelon into my hand before I could say anything. "New person!" she announced to the group, in Korean and then in crisp, careful English. They applauded. Applauded. I stood there dripping watermelon juice onto my bare feet, my mouth hanging open, while a man in an undershirt brought me a chair and someone else handed me a pair of chopsticks.

Juniper had never lived outside Georgia, and the drive to Vermont had taken three days. She was exhausted, cranky, and wrestling a mattress up a narrow staircase alone when a door on the landing opened. A man stepped out. She glanced up, ready to apologize for blocking the way, and her grip slipped. The mattress slid back down three steps and wedged itself against her shins. It was her father. Her father, whom she hadn't seen since she was seven, the man who'd moved somewhere north and stopped calling. He was older and grayer, and he was holding a watering can. They stared at each other across the landing. "June-bug?" he whispered. Nobody had called her that in twenty years. Juniper's knees went loose. She sat down on the stairs, the mattress pressing into her legs, staring up at him as if he were a ghost. He set the watering can down very slowly, as though any sudden movement might make her vanish.

The apartment in Tokyo was smaller than my closet back home. I'd known that. I'd seen the photos. But standing in it for the first time with two suitcases, I kept turning in slow circles, bumping into walls, unable to find anywhere to put anything. Then I opened what I assumed was a cupboard and nearly fell inside. It was a staircase. A narrow, steep wooden staircase leading up. I climbed it, feeling like a kid in a fairy tale, and came out into a loft with a slanted ceiling and a round window looking straight out at Mount Fuji, pink in the evening light. I sat down hard on the floorboards. The listing hadn't mentioned a loft. It hadn't mentioned a mountain. I took out my phone to call my mother and then just sat there, holding it, staring out the round window, my mouth slightly open, forgetting I had meant to dial at all.

When Obadiah's moving boxes arrived at his new place in Edinburgh, there was one more than he'd packed. He counted them twice. Seventeen. He'd packed sixteen. The extra one was taped up with old-fashioned brown paper and string, and it was addressed in his own name, in his late wife's handwriting. Obadiah sat down on a box of kitchenware so abruptly that something inside it crunched. He stared at the parcel for a long time without touching it. Then he cut the string with his pocketknife and lifted the lid. Inside was a teapot, her favorite blue teapot, wrapped in newspaper, and a note: I asked your sister to sneak this in. Don't you dare drink coffee in Scotland. Obadiah let out a sound halfway between a laugh and a sob. He turned the teapot in his hands, examining every chip, and kept reading the note over and over, his eyebrows climbing, his lips moving silently around each word.

Mile twenty-five. My legs were concrete. My lungs were sandpaper. I had stopped thinking in words a long time ago and was just counting steps, one-two, one-two, when I heard my name. Not just shouted. Sung. I looked up and nearly tripped over my own feet. Lining the barricades on both sides of the road were about thirty people in matching orange shirts with my face printed on them, and they were singing the fight song from my high school in Lagos. My old classmates. People I hadn't seen in fifteen years. I recognized Chidi, and Folake, and my old coach, who must be eighty by now, waving a cane. My mouth fell open and stayed open. I actually slowed down, which you never do in the last mile. Somebody threw a sponge at me and it hit my chest and I didn't even feel it. "How?" I gasped at them as I passed. They just sang louder.

Grete had been running in a fog for the last six miles, legs heavy, vision narrowing to the back of the runner ahead of her. With one mile to go, she glanced down at her watch, expecting to see the slow, sad number she'd been dreading since mile eighteen. She looked again. She shook her wrist. The watch said she was on pace for three hours and two minutes. Eleven minutes faster than she'd ever run in her life. Her eyes went wide. She nearly stumbled into a water table. That couldn't be right; she felt like she'd been crawling. She glanced at the clock on the mile marker as she passed, and it agreed. Grete let out a strangled noise, half gasp and half laugh, and a spectator gave her an odd look. Her legs, which a minute ago had felt like wet sandbags, suddenly had springs in them. She kept glancing at the watch every few strides, disbelieving, as though it might change its mind.

The last mile of the Boston Marathon is supposed to be a blur of noise, and it was, until I saw the dog. A scruffy brown mutt, no leash, no owner, trotting beside me on the course like he was registered. I looked around for someone chasing him. Nobody. He looked up at me with his tongue lolling, matching my pace exactly. "Where did you come from?" I panted, and he wagged. The crowd had noticed; they were pointing and cheering, and someone shouted, "Go, doggie!" I started laughing, which hurt my ribs, which made me laugh harder. Every time I tried to slow down to shoo him off, he slowed down too and sat, waiting. Every time I sped up, there he was. He crossed the finish line half a step ahead of me. A volunteer hung a medal on my neck, then, without missing a beat, hung one on the dog. I stood there, gasping, hands on my knees, completely bewildered.

Benjamín was certain the cramp in his calf would end his race. He had hobbled through mile twenty-five, grimacing, and was considering stepping off the course when a woman jogged up beside him. She was in her sixties, wiry, grey-haired, wearing a race bib and a headband. She took one look at him and said, "Calf? Here," and handed him a pickle. A whole dill pickle, wrapped in plastic. Benjamín stared at it. "Pickle juice," she said. "Trust me." Too exhausted to argue, he bit into it. Sour juice flooded his mouth, and within a minute, impossibly, the cramp loosened. He looked down at his leg as though it belonged to someone else. He looked at the woman, who was now pulling ahead with a cheerful wave. He looked at the half-eaten pickle in his hand. "Who are you?" he called after her, his voice cracking with disbelief. She just laughed over her shoulder and kept running toward the finish.

The last mile was uphill, which nobody had warned me about. I was dragging myself up it, every step a negotiation, when a little girl at the barricade held up a sign. It said GO MOM. I glanced at it, then did a double take so violent I nearly fell. It was my daughter. My daughter, who was supposed to be at her father's house in Phoenix this weekend. She was jumping up and down beside my ex-husband, who was holding a second sign: YOU'VE GOT THIS, PEARL. My ex-husband. Who had once said that running marathons was a midlife crisis with a medal. I stopped. Actually stopped, in the middle of the road, runners streaming around me. My daughter shrieked and waved. I waved back with both arms, my breath coming in big ragged gulps, tears starting from nowhere. "You came?" I yelled across the barricade. My ex just pointed toward the finish line and shouted, "Go!"

Augusto had been passing the same runner back and forth for ten miles, a tall man in a banana costume. It had become a private rivalry. In the final mile, with the banana just ahead, Augusto summoned everything he had left and pulled even. As he passed, the banana turned its head, and Augusto saw the face inside the foam. It was his doctor. His cardiologist, Dr. Nakamura, who just six months ago had told him he was lucky to be alive and that he should take up gentle walking. Augusto's legs nearly buckled. "Doctor?" he wheezed. The banana's eyes went wide too. "Mr. Pires? What are you doing here?" "What are you doing here?" Augusto shot back. They stared at each other, panting, still running side by side, neither willing to slow down. Augusto's heart, the heart the doctor had saved, was hammering, and he couldn't tell if it was from the race or from the sight of his cardiologist dressed as fruit.

I'd let Biscuit out at nine, like always, and gone to brush my teeth. When I came back and called for him, nothing. The yard was dark. I called again, louder, and stepped out onto the deck in my socks, my stomach starting to knot. The gate was latched. The fence was intact. No Biscuit. I grabbed a flashlight and swept it across the lawn, calling his name in a voice that kept rising. Then I heard it, faintly: a bark. From above me. I swung the beam up. Biscuit, my fat, lazy, eleven-year-old beagle, was sitting on the roof of the garden shed, wagging his tail at me as though it were the most natural place in the world. My jaw dropped. The flashlight beam wobbled. "How?" I said. "How did you get up there?" I could see the overturned wheelbarrow, the woodpile beside it, a ladder of sorts. He barked again, cheerfully, and I just stood there gaping.

Haruki whistled from the back door the way he always did, two sharp notes, and waited for the jingle of Momo's collar. It didn't come. He whistled again, stepping out onto the patio. The garden was quiet except for the crickets. Then he noticed the hole. A huge hole, freshly dug, under the azalea bush, with dirt sprayed across the grass in a wide fan. He walked over and peered down into it with his phone light. It wasn't a hole. It was a tunnel. It sloped down and sideways, under the fence, toward the neighbor's yard. Haruki's eyebrows shot up. He followed the line of it with the light, his mouth falling open, to where a second hole had erupted in the neighbor's lawn. Beside it, in a puddle of moonlight, sat Momo, muddy to the shoulders, curled up next to the neighbor's golden retriever, both of them looking extremely pleased with themselves. Haruki let out a low, incredulous whistle.

My dog Pepper never stays out longer than five minutes. She does her business and scratches the door to be let back in, every single time, because she hates the cold. So when twenty minutes passed, I put on my boots and went looking, calling her name across the snowy yard. I found her by the back fence, sitting perfectly still, staring at something in the bushes. I crept closer, my heart in my throat, expecting a raccoon or something worse. It was a fawn. A tiny, spotted fawn, curled in the snow, and Pepper was lying next to it, pressed against its side, keeping it warm. I stopped dead. I actually put my hand over my mouth. My grumpy, snappish old terrier, who growls at the mail carrier, who once bit my brother. She looked up at me and thumped her tail once in the snow, as if to say, well, don't just stand there. I couldn't move.

When Gloria went out to check on Rufus, she expected to find him chasing squirrels. Instead the yard was empty and the back gate stood wide open, swinging gently in the wind. Her heart lurched. She ran out into the alley in her bathrobe, shouting his name. Halfway down the block she stopped short. A small crowd had gathered on the corner, and in the middle of it sat Rufus, her rumpled old basset hound, wearing a tiny plastic firefighter's helmet. Three firefighters were taking turns patting him. Their engine sat at the curb, lights off. "Is this your dog?" one of them asked, grinning. "He wandered into the station and climbed onto the truck. We think he wants a job." Gloria stood frozen, her robe flapping, her hand pressed flat against her chest. Rufus had never walked further than the end of the driveway without being dragged. She stared at the little helmet and burst out laughing.

Dusk had fallen, and Kasimir still hadn't come in. I stood on the back step calling him, my voice getting thinner each time. Kasimir is a Great Dane. He's hard to lose. I walked the perimeter of the fence twice with a flashlight and found nothing. Then I noticed the light on in the neighbors' sunroom, and in the window, an enormous silhouette. I squinted. I took three steps closer. There was my dog, sitting upright on the neighbors' sofa, while their elderly father, Mr. Abiodun, read aloud to him from a book. Kasimir's ears were pricked forward. He looked riveted. I pressed my face almost to the glass, my breath fogging it, my eyebrows climbing toward my scalp. Mr. Abiodun looked up, saw me, and waved me inside without breaking off the sentence. "He comes every evening," he said when I stepped in. "We're on chapter nine." I stood there in their doorway, absolutely lost for words.

Sunniva assumed the worst when Klaus didn't come in for dinner. Klaus never missed dinner. She'd heard coyotes the night before, and her hands were shaking as she grabbed the lantern and ran out into the field behind the house. She followed his tracks in the mud to the old well and stopped, breathing hard. Klaus was lying beside the well, perfectly fine, with his paw resting protectively over a small cardboard box. Sunniva crept closer and lifted the flap. Inside were four kittens, eyes still closed, mewing faintly. Klaus looked up at her with mournful dignity, as though she'd interrupted something important. Sunniva sank to her knees in the wet grass, the lantern tipping beside her. Klaus hated cats. He had chased the barn cat up a tree every day for six years. She looked from the kittens to the dog and back again, her mouth hanging open, and Klaus, very gently, licked the smallest kitten's head.

The stage manager gave me the five-minute signal, and I picked up my violin and walked to the wings, breathing slow, the way my teacher taught me. I peeked out at the audience. The hall was full, as expected. What wasn't expected was the front row. My grandfather sat dead center, in his good suit, holding a program. My grandfather, who had told me for ten years that music was a hobby, not a career, who had refused to come to a single recital. He was here. He was early. He was reading the program with his glasses on the end of his nose, frowning in concentration. My bow slipped in my hand and tapped the floor. The stage manager hissed at me. I barely heard her. I just kept staring through the gap in the curtain, my heart racing, my mouth dry. Then he looked up, straight at the curtain, and winked. My knees nearly gave out right there in the wings.

Ngozi was tuning her cello backstage when the conductor came rushing in, pale and breathless. "The soloist is sick," he said. "Food poisoning. You know the Elgar?" Ngozi's tuning peg slipped and the string went slack with a twang. Of course she knew the Elgar. She had played it alone in her apartment a thousand times. But she was fourth chair, a member of the section, invisible. "Me?" she said. "In front of everyone?" "In twelve minutes," the conductor said. Ngozi stared at him. She looked down at her own hands on the cello's neck, then at her plain black concert dress, then at the door through which she could hear two thousand people murmuring. Her heartbeat was pounding in her ears so loudly she could barely hear him explaining the cuts. She nodded without knowing she was nodding. Someone pressed a glass of water into her hand. She held it without drinking, staring at the floor, her eyes enormous.

I was sitting at the piano bench waiting for the curtain to rise, running scales on my thigh to calm my fingers, when I looked down at the music stand and found someone had replaced my sheet music. My Chopin was gone. In its place was a single page, handwritten, with a note at the top: Play this instead. Please. —A. I turned the page over. Nothing. I looked around the stage, at the stagehands, at the curtain, but no one met my eyes. The melody on the page was simple, lilting, and halfway down I realized I knew it. It was the lullaby my mother used to hum, the one I'd never heard anywhere else, the one I'd assumed she made up. A was her initial. Anneliese. She'd been dead for six years. I sat frozen on the bench, my fingers hovering above the keys, my chest tight, as the curtain began to rise.

The Battle of the Bands was the biggest show Tariq's group had ever played, and he was pacing backstage, drumsticks tapping against his leg, when a woman in a headset grabbed his arm. "You're Tariq Al-Masri? Someone wants to meet you." She steered him toward a corner where a man stood in a faded leather jacket. Tariq glanced at him and then stopped walking. His drumsticks fell out of his hand and bounced across the floor. It was Jimmy Szabo. The Jimmy Szabo, drummer for Steel Harbor, the man whose posters had covered every wall of Tariq's childhood bedroom. "I saw your video online," Jimmy said, holding out a hand. "Wanted to see you play live." Tariq stared at the hand. Then at the face. He didn't move to shake it. He simply couldn't make his arm work. "You saw my video," he repeated hoarsely. Jimmy laughed and picked up the dropped drumsticks and pressed them back into Tariq's numb fingers.

Five minutes before the show, Rosemary stepped out of the dressing room to find the corridor lined with children. Dozens of them, in neat rows on either side, holding paper hearts. She stopped in the doorway, her guitar case bumping against her knee. "What's all this?" she asked, but nobody answered. They were just smiling at her, a little shyly. Then a teacher stepped forward and explained: these were the kids from the hospital ward where Rosemary had played every Thursday for two years. They had come, all of them, every one who'd been discharged, with their parents. Rosemary's hand flew to her mouth. She recognized faces. The little boy with the cast. The girl who'd asked her to play the same song eleven times in a row. Rosemary set the guitar case down without noticing and crouched to their level, blinking hard, her breath catching. "You came," she kept saying, her voice wobbling. "All of you came?"

I'd played the jazz club a hundred times, and the crowd was always the same: regulars, tourists, a couple of bored bartenders. So I wasn't paying much attention as I adjusted my saxophone strap and peered through the haze at the small round tables. Then I saw the man at table four, and the reed nearly slipped off my mouthpiece. It was Sonny Gallardo. Sonny Gallardo, who'd played with every legend I'd ever worshipped, who I thought had retired to Puerto Rico years ago. He was sitting by himself with a glass of rum, watching me. Me. I fumbled the strap. I checked the reed three times. My mouth had gone so dry I wasn't sure I could play a note. The bandleader leaned over and whispered, "Is that who I think it is?"
