I could only nod. Sonny lifted his glass to me in a tiny salute, and I felt my whole face go hot, like a boy at his first recital.

The box on my doorstep was enormous, the size of a small refrigerator, and I hadn't ordered anything in weeks. I circled it twice in my slippers, reading the label. My name, my address, no return address at all. I dragged it inside, panting, and slit the tape with a kitchen knife. Packing peanuts erupted everywhere. I dug through them up to my elbows and my fingers closed on something cold and smooth. I pulled it out and nearly dropped it. It was the brass telescope from my grandfather's study, the one that had been sold at the estate auction when I was twelve, the one I had cried about for a week. I recognized the dent near the eyepiece, from the time I'd knocked it off the windowsill. I sat down in the drift of packing peanuts, cradling it, my heart thudding. A small card fluttered out. It said only: Found it. Took me nineteen years. Love, your cousin Thaddeus.

Philomena did not get packages. She was eighty-three, lived alone, and her mail consisted entirely of electric bills and catalogs for orthopedic shoes. So when the delivery man rang her bell and handed her a small parcel wrapped in brown paper, she held it at arm's length, squinting. The postmark was from Ghana. She didn't know anyone in Ghana. She opened it at the kitchen table with her letter opener, slowly, as if it might be a bomb. Inside was a hand-carved wooden bird and a photograph of a smiling young man in a graduation gown. On the back of the photo: Dear Mrs. Philomena, you sponsored my school fees for twelve years through the church program. I am now a doctor. Thank you. Philomena's hands began to tremble. She'd forgotten. She had honestly forgotten about the twenty dollars a month. She set the photo down, picked it back up, and set it down again, her lips parted, her eyes swimming.

I heard the thud on the porch around noon and assumed it was the dog food I'd ordered. The box was the right size. But when I lifted it, something inside it shifted and made a noise. A small, indignant noise. I nearly dropped it. I set it down very carefully on the hallway floor and stared at it. It made the noise again. A chirp. Then a scratch. I knelt and peeled back the flap with two fingers, ready to leap away, and found myself looking into the eyes of a very offended baby duck. Twelve of them, actually, crowded into a heat-padded crate, along with a printed invoice for a farm supply company and a delivery address two streets over. I sat back on my heels in the hallway. A duckling climbed out of the crate and waddled onto my sock. "Hello," I said weakly, because I had no idea what else one says to a duck at noon on a Tuesday.

Sebastián tore open the padded envelope expecting the replacement phone charger he'd ordered. Instead, a cassette tape slid out onto the counter. He hadn't seen a cassette in twenty years. He turned it over. On the label, in faded pencil, someone had written: Seb & Lola, summer '98. His breath stuck in his throat. Lola. His best friend from childhood in Valparaíso, who had moved to Australia when they were eleven. That summer they had recorded themselves on her father's tape deck, singing, telling jokes, making up radio shows. He'd assumed the tape was lost forever. There was a sticky note tucked inside the case: Found this when my dad died. Thought you should have it. L. Sebastián rummaged through every drawer in the apartment, frantic, until he found his old Walkman. He pressed play with shaking fingers, and a tinny, high-pitched voice said, "Good evening, this is Radio Seb," and he sat straight down on the kitchen floor.

The package was addressed to my mother, who has been dead for four years. I almost sent it back. Instead I stood at the mailbox in the rain turning it over and over, my umbrella dripping onto the cardboard. It was postmarked from a jewelry repair shop in Krakow. I carried it inside and opened it at the kitchen table. Inside was a small velvet pouch, and inside that was my mother's wedding ring, the one we'd searched the whole house for after the funeral. There was a receipt dated five years ago, a repair ticket for a broken clasp, and a note from the jeweler: Apologies for the long delay. We had a flood. I made a sound I'd never made before, a sort of gasp that turned into a hiccup. I put the ring on my palm and stared at it. All this time it had been sitting on a shelf in Poland, waiting. I couldn't stop turning it in the lamplight.

Rashida had been home sick for three days, wrapped in blankets, miserable. When the doorbell rang she shuffled to answer it in her pajamas and found a box on the step, the size of a toaster, with her name on it in a child's crayon writing. She frowned. She brought it inside and sat on the couch to open it. Inside were dozens of folded paper cranes in every color, a jar of honey, and a stack of drawings. Every drawing showed a woman with big hair, which she slowly realized was supposed to be her. GET WELL MS. RASHIDA, one said, in shaky capitals. Her second-grade class. They'd all signed it. Thirty-one names. Rashida's eyebrows lifted higher and higher as she unfolded each drawing, her blocked nose forgotten. One showed her riding a dinosaur. One showed her with wings. She pressed a hand to her chest, laughing, then coughing, then laughing again, shaking her head in utter disbelief.

My brother and I had been sorting Nana's closet for an hour, folding cardigans into bags for the charity shop, when Cyprian shook out an old wool coat and something heavy fell from the lining. It hit the floor with a clink. We both looked down. A tiny drawstring pouch. I picked it up and loosened the string, and a handful of gold coins slid into my palm. Old ones, with a king's face on them. Cyprian made a choked sound. I held my hand perfectly still, afraid that if I moved, the coins would vanish. "Nana," I said. "Nana, who reused tea bags?" He took the coat back and felt along the hem, and his eyes widened. "There's more," he whispered. The lining was stitched full of them. We sat down on her bed, side by side, the coat across both our laps, and neither of us said anything for a long time. Every so often one of us would laugh, briefly, and then stop.

Kalinda and her younger sister Vanessa had agreed to split their grandmother's recipe boxes, and they'd been bickering amiably over who got the cornbread card. When Kalinda lifted the last box, its false bottom slid out and a packet of photographs fanned across the kitchen table. The sisters leaned in together. The pictures showed their grandmother as a young woman, maybe twenty, standing on a stage in a sequined costume. In one she was mid-leap. In another she was being lifted overhead by a tall man in a top hat. Vanessa grabbed Kalinda's wrist. "Is that Grandma?" Kalinda nodded slowly, her mouth open. She turned one over. Written on the back in pencil: Harlem, 1949, opening night. Their grandmother, who had worn orthopedic shoes and attended church three times a week, who had told them dancing was a waste of time. The sisters stared at each other across the scattered photographs, their recipe argument completely forgotten.

The jewelry box was supposed to be easy. Nana's costume jewelry, all of it cheap and sparkly and sentimental. My sister Liesel and I took turns choosing pieces, crying a little, laughing a little. Then I lifted the velvet tray out of the bottom of the box, looking for stray earrings, and found a folded document. It was a birth certificate. The name on it was not my grandmother's. The name was Hannelore Weiss, born 1931 in Munich. Liesel took it out of my hands and read it twice, frowning. "Who's Hannelore?" she asked. Underneath the certificate was a passport photo of a young girl with Nana's exact nose, Nana's exact eyes. And a second passport, with a different name, the name we'd always known. I felt dizzy and had to put a hand on the dresser. Our grandmother, who had told us she was born in Ohio, had arrived somehow as someone else entirely. We looked at each other, neither of us breathing.

Three brothers stood in their grandmother's garage, staring at the shape under the tarp. They'd assumed it was her old sedan. Alejandro, the eldest, grabbed a corner and pulled. The tarp slid away to reveal a gleaming red motorcycle, vintage, polished to a mirror shine, with a sidecar. Nobody spoke. Mateo, the youngest, walked all the way around it slowly, his hands hovering above the chrome without touching it. "She had a motorcycle?" he finally said, his voice cracking. Alejandro found a logbook tucked into the sidecar. He flipped through it. Dates and places. Big Sur. Moab. The Yukon. The last entry was only eight months ago. "She rode it to the coast in March," Alejandro read aloud. The middle brother, Joaquín, had to sit down on a paint can. Their grandmother had told them every Sunday that she spent her weekends gardening. They looked at each other in the dim garage and burst out laughing, helplessly, all three at once.

I didn't expect anything interesting in Oma's sewing basket. It was the last thing to sort, and my brother Florian and I were both tired and sore from hauling boxes. I tipped it upside down onto the bed to empty it, and spools and thimbles bounced everywhere. And a thick envelope addressed to both of us. Florian picked it up, glanced at me, and opened it. Inside was a letter in Oma's spidery hand and two lottery tickets. Old ones. The letter said: I won this in 1987. I never cashed it. I thought you two would have more fun deciding what to do with it than I would. Florian's eyes went huge. He held one ticket up to the light, then the other. "Is this real?" he whispered. I grabbed my phone and started searching the numbers, my thumbs clumsy. Oma, who darned her socks. Who saved string. I could feel my pulse jumping in my neck.

Eleni and her brother Stavros had been dreading the attic. When they finally climbed up there with flashlights, they expected cobwebs and old suitcases. Instead their beams landed on a wall covered floor to ceiling with paintings. Oil paintings, dozens of them, landscapes of their grandmother's island, the harbor, the white houses, the sea at every hour of the day. Stavros swung his flashlight slowly from one canvas to the next, his mouth falling open. "Did you know?" he asked. Eleni shook her head. She couldn't speak. She stepped closer to one painting and saw the initials in the corner: E.P. Eleni Papadakis. Their grandmother. The woman she was named for. In forty years she had never once seen her pick up a brush. Eleni put her hand flat against her own chest as if to keep something inside from escaping. She and Stavros stood in the dusty silence, turning in circles, their flashlight beams crossing and recrossing the canvases.

I unlocked the shop at seven-thirty like every Monday, flicked on the lights, and stopped with my hand still on the switch. The entire ceiling was covered in balloons. Not a few. Hundreds of them, pastel colors, ribbons dangling down to head height like jellyfish tentacles. I stood in the doorway with my keys dangling from one finger. The alarm hadn't gone off. The door had been locked. I walked in slowly, ribbons brushing my face, and found a banner strung across the register: TEN YEARS! WE LOVE YOU, MRS. NGUYEN. Underneath it was a pile of cards from my customers, the regulars, the kids who bought candy after school, the old man who came in for the same newspaper every morning. My landlord must have let them in. My hand went to my mouth. I'd completely forgotten the date. I sat down on the stool behind the counter and just stared up at the ceiling, blinking, one ribbon tickling my nose.

Every Monday, Gustavo opened his bookshop to an empty street. That was the rhythm of it. But this morning, as he fumbled with the key in the cold, he heard murmuring behind him and turned around. There was a line. An actual line of people, stretching from his door down past the bakery and around the corner. Gustavo's key slipped out of the lock and fell onto the doormat. He bent to pick it up without taking his eyes off the crowd. "Can I help you?" he called, his voice coming out strangely high. A young woman near the front held up her phone. "You're the shop from the video," she said. Someone had filmed his cat sleeping in the poetry section and posted it online over the weekend, and apparently half the city had seen it. Gustavo looked at the phone, then at the line, then at his cat, who was watching from the window, utterly indifferent. He laughed out loud.

I knew something was off before I even got out of the car. The window of my flower shop was different, brighter. I walked up to it with my coffee and nearly spilled it down my front. Someone had painted a mural across the whole storefront glass overnight: sunflowers, tulips, a sky full of bees, and in the middle, a cartoon of me, apron and glasses and all, holding a watering can. I set my coffee down on the sidewalk without thinking about it and stepped back into the street to see the whole thing. A delivery van honked and I jumped back onto the curb. The detail was incredible. Every petal shaded. My glasses even had the crack in the left lens. In the corner was a signature: Thanks for the free roses, love Jasmine, age 15. The girl who swept my floors on Saturdays. I stood on the sidewalk with my mouth hanging open, people slowing down to look at the window, then at me.

Mr. Adeyemi had owned the hardware store for thirty-one years and opened it the same way every Monday: lights, coffee, radio, broom. He was halfway through sweeping when he noticed the envelope on the counter. It had not been there on Saturday night. He set the broom against the shelf and picked it up carefully. Inside was a stack of cash and a note in block letters: I took a hammer and a box of nails from your store when I was fourteen. I'm sorry. This is with interest. Mr. Adeyemi counted the bills. Then counted again. Five hundred dollars. He looked up at the door, which had been locked all weekend, and then noticed the mail slot. His eyebrows rose slowly. He turned the note over looking for a name, found none, and sat down on the step stool behind the counter. The radio played softly. He sat there with the money in his lap, shaking his head, chuckling under his breath.

The sign on the door said OPEN, but I hadn't flipped it yet. I stood outside my café on the sidewalk, frowning at it, keys halfway out of my pocket. Through the window I could see the lights on and someone moving behind the counter. My heart jumped into my throat. I grabbed my phone, ready to call the police, and then the door swung open and my son stepped out with a dish towel over his shoulder. My son, who was supposed to be at university in Montreal, who hadn't been home since Christmas. "Morning, Papa," he said, grinning. "Espresso's ready." My phone nearly slid out of my hand. "Rémy?" I said. "How did you get a key?" "Maman," he said, and winked. I stepped inside slowly. The pastries were out. The tables were wiped. He'd even written the specials on the chalkboard, in the same loopy handwriting he'd used as a child. I just stood there in the doorway, stammering.

Cordelia expected the usual Monday mess when she unlocked the antique shop: a weekend's worth of dust and the faint smell of old furniture. She did not expect the grandfather clock to be ticking. That clock hadn't worked since before she bought the shop, eleven years ago. She had paid three different repairmen to look at it, and every one of them had shrugged and said it was hopeless. Now its pendulum swung steadily, and as she stood frozen in the doorway, it began to chime eight o'clock. Cordelia dropped her handbag. She walked slowly toward the clock, her heels tapping on the wooden floor, half afraid it would stop if she came too close. On the little ledge inside the case, she found a tiny screwdriver and a handwritten tag: Just needed a new suspension spring. —Elias, your new upstairs neighbor. Cordelia read the tag twice, then stood listening to the chimes ring out, her hand pressed to her collarbone, and, to her own bewilderment, burst into giggles.

My first shift at the food bank, they put me on canned goods sorting. Simple enough: beans here, soup there, check the expiration dates. I was working through a donation box when I pulled out a can and froze. It wasn't soup. It was a can, all right, but the label had been peeled off and replaced with a handwritten one: For whoever opens this: look inside the box flap. I glanced around. Nobody was watching. I checked the flap of the cardboard box and found an envelope taped there, and inside it, four hundred dollars in cash and a note: Use this for fresh fruit. Kids need more than cans. I stood perfectly still in the middle of the warehouse, the envelope in one hand and the can in the other. The coordinator, a woman named Hortensia, came over to ask if I was okay, and I just held the envelope out to her. Her eyebrows flew up.

Brother Anselm had volunteered at the food bank every Thursday for nine years, and he knew every face in the line. So when he looked up from the bread table and saw a woman in a tailored coat and pearl earrings, he paused with a loaf in midair. Then he recognized her. It was Mrs. Fairweather, the wealthiest donor in the parish, whose name was carved into the stone above the church hall. She met his eyes, flushed scarlet, and held out a canvas bag. "My husband's business failed," she said quietly. "Nobody knows yet." Anselm's mouth opened, then closed. The loaf of bread was still suspended in his hand. He had a sudden memory of her at the Christmas gala, laughing in a velvet gown. He lowered the bread into her bag very gently, as though it were made of glass. "Thank you, Brother," she whispered. He watched her walk away, his hand still hovering above the table.

I was stacking cereal boxes in the back when one of the regular clients, a little boy of about seven, tugged on my apron and handed me a jar. A jam jar, full of coins and crumpled bills. "For the food bank," he said solemnly. "I saved it." I crouched down to his level, the jar heavy in my hands, and blinked at him. This was a kid whose family came every single week. Whose mother counted every item into the bag twice. "Where did you get all this?" I asked, and my voice came out thin. He explained that he'd been collecting cans from the park and returning them for the deposit. For months. I looked down at the jar again, at the pennies and nickels and one single folded ten. My throat felt tight. I didn't know what to say. I stayed there on my knees on the concrete floor, holding the jar in both hands like something sacred, staring at this small, serious person.

Yolanda was handing out bags of rice when a man in a frayed jacket reached the front of the line and said, "Miss Torres?" She glanced up. He was maybe thirty, unshaven, with a familiar dimple. "It's Kevin," he said. "Kevin Mbeki. Fourth grade. You taught me to read." The rice bag slipped in her grip. She caught it against her stomach. Kevin. The boy who'd hidden in the coat closet during reading time, who'd cried when she first made him read aloud. The boy who'd written her a thank-you card at the end of the year in big wobbly letters. She'd always wondered what had become of him. "Kevin?" she said, her voice going up at the end. She came around the table without thinking, still clutching the rice, and stood in front of him, searching his face. He laughed, embarrassed, and pulled a battered paperback from his jacket pocket. "Still reading," he said. Yolanda covered her mouth with her free hand.

The delivery truck was supposed to bring the usual pallet of canned vegetables. I signed for it on my clipboard, half paying attention, and went to open the back. The driver grinned at me. "You'll want to see this," he said. He rolled up the door, and I took an involuntary step back. The truck was full of turkeys. Frozen turkeys, stacked to the ceiling, hundreds of them, frost steaming in the morning air. "Who sent these?" I said. He handed me a slip. The sender was a man named Lionel Ashby, and the note said: For the people who fed my family in 1992. I had to lean against the tailgate. 1992. The food bank had been in a church basement then, run by my mother. I'd been nine years old, stacking cans just like now. I stared at the turkeys, my breath coming out in little clouds, and kept saying, "Hundreds," under my breath, as if counting them might help.

Bao had signed up to volunteer at the food bank to pad his college applications. He wasn't proud of it, but that was the truth. On his first day, the coordinator assigned him to help a client load groceries into her car, and he grabbed the cart without much interest and followed her out to the parking lot. Then she turned around and pulled down her scarf, and Bao stopped walking so abruptly the cart rolled into his shins. It was Ms. Delgado. His guidance counselor. The woman who would write his recommendation letter. She smiled at him, a little tight, a little embarrassed. "Hello, Bao," she said quietly, and Bao swallowed hard. She explained that her husband had been sick, and the bills had piled up. Bao stood there in the parking lot, his ears hot, his hands gripping the cart handle. He'd thought adults like her had everything figured out. He loaded the bags in silence, still reeling.

The waiting room television was stuck on a cooking show, and I'd been staring at it for two hours without taking in a single recipe. My father was in surgery. Bypass. The doctors had said it could take five hours. So when the double doors swung open after only two and a half, my stomach dropped through the floor. I stood up too fast and knocked over my coffee. The surgeon walked toward me pulling off her cap, and she was smiling. "We didn't need to do the bypass," she said. "Once we got in there, a stent was enough. He's awake. He's asking for pudding." I stared at her. Coffee was soaking into my sock. "Pudding?" I repeated, like it was a word in a foreign language. She nodded. I sat back down, missing the chair slightly, and caught myself on the armrest. My father, who had said goodbye to me that morning like he was going off to war, wanted pudding.

Ottoline had been sitting in the ER waiting room for four hours with a sprained wrist, watching the clock, irritated. When the triage nurse finally called her name, she stood and walked toward the desk, and then stopped dead. The nurse was her daughter. Her daughter Clementine, who had dropped out of college two years ago, who had told her mother she was "figuring things out," who barely returned phone calls. Clementine was wearing navy scrubs and a hospital badge. She looked up from the clipboard and saw her mother, and the clipboard tilted in her hands. "Mum?" "You're a nurse?" Ottoline said. Her voice came out so loud that half the waiting room looked up. Clementine flushed. "I was going to tell you at Christmas," she said. "When I passed the boards." Ottoline lowered her injured wrist slowly, forgetting entirely that it hurt, and stared at the badge, at the scrubs, at her daughter's capable hands.

It had been three hours since they'd wheeled my wife into the delivery room, and they'd sent me out to wait because of complications. I was sitting on a plastic chair, hands clasped so hard my knuckles ached, staring at the linoleum. When the nurse came out, I shot to my feet. "She's fine," the nurse said quickly. "And so are they." I blinked. "They?" The nurse's face did something complicated. "You didn't know?" "Know what?" I asked. My voice cracked. "Twins," she said. "A boy and a girl." I sat back down. Not on purpose; my legs just folded. We'd had three ultrasounds. Three. Each time, one heartbeat, one tiny curled shape. The nurse explained that the second baby had been hiding behind the first, which apparently happens. I barely heard her. I had painted one nursery. Bought one crib. Picked one name. I put my face in my hands and started laughing, helplessly, into my palms.

Wilfred had been staring at the same page of the same magazine for an hour when a young woman sat down next to him and began, very quietly, to cry. He glanced over, awkward, unsure whether to offer a tissue. Then he noticed her hand. On the third finger she wore a ring, a thin gold band with a tiny sapphire. His wife's ring. He'd know it anywhere; he'd chosen it himself in 1971. His wife had lost it on a beach in Cornwall in 1985 and they'd searched the sand for three days. Wilfred's magazine slid off his knees onto the floor. He couldn't take his eyes off the ring. "Excuse me," he said, his voice strangely hoarse. "Where did you get that?" The young woman sniffed and looked down at it. "My grandmother found it on a beach," she said. "In Cornwall. Years ago." Wilfred gripped the armrest, feeling the room tilt gently, his mouth hanging open in disbelief.

I'd been in the waiting room since midnight, waiting for news of my brother after his motorcycle accident. By four a.m. I'd stopped looking up every time the doors opened. So I didn't notice the man in scrubs until he was standing right in front of me, saying my name. I looked up, exhausted, and my mouth fell open. It was Marlon. Marlon Achebe, my ex-boyfriend from fifteen years ago, the one who'd dumped me to go to medical school in Edinburgh. He was a trauma surgeon now, apparently. He was the one who had been operating on my brother all night. "He's going to be okay," he said gently. "He's lucky." I just stared at him, at the gray in his temples, at the surgical mask dangling around his neck. My brain refused to connect the boy who used to steal my fries with the man who'd just saved my brother's life. "You?" I said, stupidly. He nodded, smiling crookedly. I couldn't stop staring.

Mrs. Bhattacharya had brought her knitting to the hospital waiting room because she assumed her husband's routine procedure would take the usual hour. It had been ninety minutes when a volunteer in a pink smock approached her holding a clipboard. Mrs. Bhattacharya set down her needles, bracing herself. But the volunteer only said, "Your husband asked me to give you this." She handed over a folded paper napkin. Mrs. Bhattacharya opened it. Inside, scrawled in her husband's familiar lopsided handwriting, were the words: Will you marry me again? Fifty years next week. Her knitting slid off her lap and rolled under the chair. She read the napkin twice, then looked up at the volunteer, who was grinning. "He wrote this," Mrs. Bhattacharya said, "before the anesthesia?" The volunteer nodded. "He made me promise to wait until he was out." Mrs. Bhattacharya pressed the napkin to her chest, her eyes wide, a startled laugh bubbling up out of her.
